body:
OBJECTIVES
- Students interpret a multiplication equation as a comparison and represent comparison statements as equations (4.OA.A.1).
- Students multiply or divide to solve word problems involving multiplicative comparison, distinguishing it from additive comparison (4.OA.A.2).
- Students solve multistep word problems with whole numbers, interpret remainders, and check answers with estimation (4.OA.A.3).
- Students multiply a whole number of up to four digits by a one-digit number and two two-digit numbers using place value strategies and area models (4.NBT.B.5).
- Students find quotients and remainders with up to four-digit dividends and one-digit divisors using place value strategies, and explain with models (4.NBT.B.6).

MATERIALS
- Grid paper for area models
- Base-ten blocks (flats, rods and units)
- Counters or cubes for sharing problems
- A strategy anchor chart: area model, partial products, and division by parts

FIVE-DAY PLAN
Day 1: Read Big Numbers, Smart Strategies. Model 6 × 43 with base-ten blocks, then as an area model. Lesson: Multiplying with Area Models.
Day 2: Comparison mini-lesson: "times as many" versus "more than" with cube towers (3 times as tall as 4 cubes versus 3 more than 4 cubes). Assignment: Times as Many.
Day 3: Division by parts with base-ten blocks: 96 ÷ 4, then 158 ÷ 6 with a remainder. Start Sharing and Remainders.
Day 4: Remainder talk: three stories with 75 ÷ 8 (round up for vans, drop it for full pieces, report it for leftovers). Finish Sharing and Remainders.
Day 5: Assessment: Multiplication and Division Check.

DIFFERENTIATION
- Support: give partially drawn area models with the place value parts labeled; allow a multiplication chart for basic facts so the focus stays on place value.
- Support: act out remainder stories with counters before writing equations.
- Stretch: solve 23 × 15 three different ways and explain which is most efficient; or find all the factor pairs of 72.
- Multilingual learners: highlight the key phrases "times as many," "more than," "left over" and "each" with pictures, and have students retell each story problem before solving.

FAMILY NOTE (send home at the start of the unit)
We are multiplying and dividing bigger numbers by breaking them into parts. To find 6 × 43, your child might find 6 × 40 and 6 × 3, then add them. Ask your child to show you an area model! Remainders come up in real life too: if 30 crackers are shared by 4 people, how many does each get, and how many are left?
title: Teacher guide: Multiplying and Dividing Bigger Numbers
